title: Time & How Often
description: How often and exactly when: always and rarely, earlier today and just now, the day after tomorrow, since, until and for, and the little time words that keep a story moving.

items.registerNotes: Before the verb or describing word: Dia selalu terlambat (He's always late).
Casually just kadang: Kadang aku masak sendiri (Sometimes I cook for myself).
Gentler than a flat never: Saya jarang minum kopi (I don't drink coffee much).
Pernah ke Bali? (Have you been to Bali?) is answered Pernah, or Belum pernah (not yet).
items.pitfallNote: It marks an experience, not the past in general: Saya pernah tinggal di Jakarta means you've lived there at some point.

items.registerNotes: Casually nggak pernah. For something you haven't done but still might, belum pernah (not yet) sounds more natural.
A little formal: in announcements, on signs (Segera hadir, Coming soon) and from staff. Casually people say langsung or secepatnya.
Anything earlier today: tadi pagi (this morning, now over), tadi malam (last night).
items.pitfallNote: Tadi is always past. For later today, use nanti: nanti sore (this afternoon, still to come).

items.registerNotes: Leans casual: Dia barusan pergi (She's just left). The neutral equivalent is baru saja.
Kemarin lusa is the day before yesterday.
Depan (front) makes 'next': bulan depan (next month), tahun depan (next year).
Lalu (past) works the same way: minggu lalu, tahun lalu. In speech kemarin stretches too: bulan kemarin, tahun kemarin.

items.english: in the past, once; first (before something else)
items.registerNotes: Dulu saya tinggal di Wellington (I used to live in Wellington). The formal form is dahulu.
items.pitfallNote: After a verb it means first: Saya makan dulu (I'll eat first). Saya pamit dulu, said when leaving, is 'I'll be off now'.
Nanti malam is tonight, still to come; tadi malam is last night. Malam ini also means tonight.

items.english: a moment, for a short while
items.registerNotes: Sebentar, ya (Just a moment) is what you'll hear on the phone and at counters. Casually bentar.
Lama-lama kamu terbiasa (You'll get used to it in time) is a common bit of encouragement.
Said on its own with relief when something long-awaited happens. In a story it means 'so in the end': Akhirnya kami naik taksi.
Usually at the start: Tiba-tiba listriknya mati (Suddenly the power went off).

items.pitfallNote: Sejak needs a starting point: sejak tahun lalu, sejak kecil (since I was little). For a length of time use sudah: Saya sudah dua tahun di sini.

items.registerNotes: Until: Saya kerja sampai jam lima. Arrive: Sudah sampai? (Are you there yet?), the message people send to check you got home safely.

items.pitfallNote: English 'for' with a length of time isn't untuk: Saya di sini selama dua minggu (I'm here for two weeks).

items.registerNotes: Casually tiap hari. Setiap goes with any time word: setiap minggu, setiap pagi.
Casually akhir-akhir ini: Akhir-akhir ini saya sibuk sekali (I've been really busy lately).
Terima kasih sebelumnya (Thanks in advance) ends many messages that ask for help.
Saying pagi twice makes it early: Besok pagi-pagi kita berangkat (We'll set off early tomorrow morning).
items.cultureNote: Days start early, while it's still cool: traditional markets are at their busiest first thing.
